title: How We Got the Bible
question: The Bible was written thousands of years ago, copied by hand for centuries and then translated into hundreds of languages. How did it reach us, and how close is what we read to what was first written?
plainAnswer: The Bible did not arrive as one finished book. Much of it began as spoken stories, songs, laws and sermons that were written down over roughly a thousand years, first on scrolls and later in bound books called codices. For centuries scribes copied it by hand, and while they made small mistakes, they also guarded it carefully, and we now have thousands of old copies to compare. Scholars called textual critics compare those copies to work out the earliest wording; they agree that the great majority of differences are tiny, while a small number of passages are genuinely uncertain and are flagged in modern Bibles. Translators then turn that text into other languages, and chapter and verse numbers were added much later, in the Middle Ages and the 1500s, to make finding things easier.
keyTakeaways: The Bible was written by many people over about a thousand years, often after a period of oral telling and in stages.
Before printing (c. 1455) every copy was made by hand, so copies differ; textual criticism is the careful comparison of those copies.
The Dead Sea Scrolls (found from 1947) showed that the main Hebrew text had been copied very faithfully for about a thousand years, and also that other forms of some books existed in Jesus' day.
There are about 5,800 or more Greek New Testament manuscripts, far more than for any other ancient book, though most are medieval and many are fragments.
Most textual differences are spelling, word order or slips of the pen; a few longer passages (such as Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11) are marked as doubtful in most modern Bibles.
Which books belong in the Bible (the canon) was settled gradually by use and recognition, not by one vote.
Chapter divisions date from about 1205 and New Testament verse numbers from 1551; they are helpful tools, not part of the original text.

sections.heading: Before the writing: memory, speech and early records
sections.body:
In the ancient world most people could not read, and important things were passed on by careful repetition. Families recited stories, priests taught laws, and communities sang psalms in worship. Israel was told to repeat God's words at home and on the road, and to write them on doorposts (Deut 6:6-9).

The Bible also mentions writing very early. Moses is told to write a record of a battle 'in a book' (Exod 17:14) and writes down the words of the covenant (Exod 24:4); Joshua writes in 'the book of the law of God' (Josh 24:26). So oral teaching and writing existed side by side for a long time.

The New Testament shows the same pattern. Paul hands on a summary of the gospel that he himself 'received' (1 Cor 15:3-7), a phrase used for passing on fixed teaching. Luke says that many had already written accounts based on eyewitnesses and that he investigated carefully before writing his own (Luke 1:1-4).

How long the oral stage lasted, and how much stories changed during it, is debated. Many scholars think books such as the Pentateuch grew in stages from older sources; others hold that Moses wrote most of it with later editing. For the Gospels, scholars disagree about how stable oral tradition was, with writers such as Richard Bauckham stressing named eyewitnesses and others stressing community shaping.

sources.author: Richard Bauckham
sources.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses

sources.author: Kenneth E. Bailey
sources.title: Informal Controlled Oral Tradition and the Synoptic Gospels (Asia Journal of Theology 5)

callout.text: Myth: 'Oral tradition works like the telephone game.' Fact: the party game is designed to produce errors, with one hearing and no correction. Ancient communities repeated material many times, in groups, with teachers who could correct mistakes. Scholars still debate how much flexibility there was, but the telephone game is not a fair model.

sections.heading: Scrolls, codices and scribes
sections.body:
Early biblical books were written on scrolls: long strips of papyrus (made from a reed plant) or of leather and parchment (prepared animal skin), rolled around a stick. Jeremiah dictated his prophecies to his scribe Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll; when the king burned it column by column, they wrote it all again with more added (Jer 36:4, Jer 36:32).

A scribe was a trained writer and copyist. Ezra is called 'a ready scribe in the law of Moses' (Ezra 7:6). Paul used a secretary for at least some letters: 'I Tertius, who wrote this epistle' greets the readers of Romans (Rom 16:22), and Paul sometimes added a closing line in his own hand (Gal 6:11).

Christians very early preferred the codex, the ancestor of the modern book, with pages stacked and bound. It was cheaper, held more and made it easier to find a passage. Paul asks Timothy to bring 'the books, but especially the parchments' (2 Tim 4:13). By the 300s parchment codices could hold the whole Bible in one volume.

sections.heading: The Hebrew Bible: from scrolls to the Masoretic text
sections.body:
The Old Testament was written mostly in Hebrew, with some chapters of Daniel and Ezra in Aramaic. Hebrew was written with consonants only; readers supplied the vowels from memory and reading custom. When Ezra read the law publicly, Levites helped people understand it, giving the sense (Neh 8:8).

Between roughly AD 600 and 1000 a group of Jewish scholars known as the Masoretes (from a word meaning 'tradition') added vowel signs, accent marks and notes in the margins. They counted letters and words and recorded unusual spellings so that copyists would not 'correct' them. The text they handed on is called the Masoretic Text, and it is the basis of almost all modern Old Testament translations.

The oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts are medieval: the Aleppo Codex (about 930, now partly missing) and the Leningrad Codex (dated 1008 or 1009), the oldest complete Hebrew Bible. Before 1947 that meant our full Hebrew copies were about a thousand years later than the last Old Testament books.

sources.author: Emanuel Tov
sources.title: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible

sources.author: Ernst Würthwein (rev. Alexander Fischer)
sources.title: The Text of the Old Testament

sections.heading: The Dead Sea Scrolls: a thousand-year check
sections.body:
In 1947 a Bedouin shepherd found jars of scrolls in a cave near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded remains of about 900 scrolls, of which over 200 are copies of biblical books. Every Old Testament book except Esther is represented, at least in fragments. Most date from about 250 BC to AD 68.

The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), copied around 125 BC, is complete. When compared with the medieval Masoretic Isaiah, the two agree very closely: most differences are spelling, small grammatical forms and occasional words. This showed that the scribes behind the Masoretic Text had copied with remarkable care for about a millennium.

The scrolls also showed something less often mentioned: in Jesus' day more than one form of some books circulated. A Qumran Jeremiah (4QJer-b) matches the shorter form of the book known from the Greek Septuagint. A Samuel scroll (4QSam-a) contains a paragraph about King Nahash that is missing from the Masoretic text but is described by Josephus; some modern versions such as the NRSV include it before 1 Sam 11:1. At Deut 32:8 the scrolls read 'sons of God' where the Masoretic Text has 'sons of Israel'.

So the honest summary is two-sided: the main text was stable and well preserved, and there was also real variety in some books that modern scholars weigh book by book.

callout.text: Two opposite myths. 'The Dead Sea Scrolls proved the Old Testament is word-for-word identical to the originals' overstates it: some books existed in different editions. 'The scrolls showed the Bible was rewritten' is also wrong: they confirmed that the Masoretic tradition was copied with great accuracy.

sections.heading: The Septuagint and the New Testament manuscripts
sections.body:
From about the 200s BC Jews in Alexandria translated their scriptures into Greek. This translation is called the Septuagint (Latin for 'seventy', after a legend of 70 or 72 translators). It became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the early church, and New Testament writers often quote it.

The New Testament books were written in Greek, roughly between AD 50 and 100. Letters were copied and passed between churches: Paul asks the Colossians to swap letters with Laodicea (Col 4:16), and 2 Peter already speaks of Paul's letters as a group (2 Pet 3:15-16).

None of the original documents (autographs) survives; that is true of virtually every ancient book. What survives are copies. Scholars now list about 5,800 to 5,900 Greek New Testament manuscripts, from scraps to complete Bibles, plus thousands of early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic and others) and countless quotations in early Christian writers.

Notable examples: P52, a scrap of John 18 usually dated to the first half or middle of the 100s (some scholars argue for a wider range, into the 200s); P46, a collection of Paul's letters from about 200; and the great parchment Bibles Codex Vaticanus (about 300-350) and Codex Sinaiticus (about 330-360).

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman
sources.title: The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration

sources.author: Brent Nongbri
sources.title: The Use and Abuse of P52 (Harvard Theological Review 98)

sources.author: Institute for New Testament Textual Research, Münster
sources.title: Kurzgefasste Liste der griechischen Handschriften des Neuen Testaments (online register)

callout.text: Counting manuscripts sounds impressive, but most Greek copies are from after AD 800. What matters more is how many early witnesses there are, and here too the New Testament is far better attested than other ancient texts, with dozens of papyri from before 300.

sections.heading: Textual criticism in plain words
sections.body:
Textual criticism means comparing copies to work out what the original most likely said. 'Criticism' here means careful judgement, not attack. A textual critic asks: which reading is found in the oldest and most widespread copies? Which reading best explains how the others arose? Which is the kind of change a tired or well-meaning scribe would make?

Most variants are trivial: spelling, word order (Greek word order is flexible), a missing 'the', or a scribe skipping a line because two lines ended the same way. Very few affect meaning, and scholars across the spectrum agree that no central Christian teaching depends on a disputed reading alone.

A few are larger and are marked in modern Bibles. The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is missing from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from the earliest Greek copies of John, though many scholars think it is an old, true story. The 'three heavenly witnesses' at 1 John 5:7 in the King James Version comes from late Latin copies and is almost universally regarded as an addition. Others include Luke 22:43-44 and Acts 8:37.

Where scholars disagree is in tone and implications. Bart Ehrman (*Misquoting Jesus*, 2005) stresses that scribes sometimes changed the text deliberately and that we cannot always be sure of the original. Daniel Wallace and others respond that the sheer number of copies lets us recover the original wording with high confidence in nearly every place. Some, such as David Parker, prefer to speak of a 'living text' and question whether a single original is always the right goal.

callout.text: Scholars agree on the facts (how many variants, which passages are doubtful). They disagree about emphasis: whether the glass is 'nearly full' (we can recover the text with high confidence) or whether the uncertainties, though small, should make us more cautious about speaking of 'the original'.

sections.heading: Which books? A short note on the canon
sections.body:
'Canon' comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod. It means the list of books a community treats as Scripture. Jesus refers to the Hebrew scriptures as 'the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44), a three-part grouping close to the later Jewish one.

For the New Testament, the four Gospels and Paul's letters were widely accepted by the late 100s. A few books (Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation) were questioned in some regions for longer. The first list exactly matching today's 27 books is in a letter of Athanasius of Alexandria in 367. Regional councils in North Africa (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) endorsed the same New Testament list.

Christians still differ over the Old Testament: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra books (the deuterocanon) that Protestant Bibles omit or place in a separate section. The companion guide 'Why some books were left out' tells that story in detail.

sections.heading: Translations: from Greek and Latin to every language
sections.body:
The Bible has been translated from the start: the Septuagint into Greek, then Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Ethiopic and more. Jerome's Latin translation, begun around 382 at the request of Pope Damasus and largely finished by about 405, became known as the Vulgate ('common version') and was the Bible of Western Europe for a thousand years.

In England, followers of John Wycliffe produced English Bibles from the Latin in the 1380s and 1390s. Printing changed everything: the Gutenberg Bible (a Latin Bible) appeared about 1455, and Erasmus printed the Greek New Testament in 1516. William Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek into English (1526) and was executed in 1536. Martin Luther's German New Testament appeared in 1522 and his complete Bible in 1534. The King James Version of 1611 drew heavily on Tyndale.

Modern translations use older manuscripts discovered since 1611 and differ in approach. 'Formal equivalence' tries to keep close to the original words and structure (for example the ESV or NASB). 'Dynamic' or 'functional equivalence' aims to convey the same meaning in natural modern speech (for example the NLT or GNT). Most translations sit somewhere between. Every translation involves choices, which is why comparing several is a good habit.

sources.author: David Daniell
sources.title: The Bible in English: Its History and Influence

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger
sources.title: The Bible in Translation: Ancient and English Versions

callout.text: Myth: 'Modern Bibles have removed verses.' Fact: modern translations follow older manuscripts that do not contain some lines later added in medieval copies. Most print those lines in brackets or footnotes so readers can see them. Whether the older or the majority of later manuscripts should be preferred is debated by a minority who favour the Byzantine or 'Textus Receptus' tradition.

sections.heading: Chapter and verse: a medieval convenience
sections.body:
The original books had no chapter or verse numbers. Hebrew scrolls did have paragraph breaks and, by the Masoretic period, marked verse endings, but no numbers.

The chapter divisions most Bibles use are usually credited to Stephen Langton, who taught in Paris before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 1207; they were added to Latin Bibles around 1205. Numbered verses in the Hebrew Bible go back to a Hebrew concordance by Rabbi Isaac Nathan in the 1440s. The Paris printer Robert Estienne (Stephanus) added New Testament verse numbers in his Greek New Testament of 1551, reportedly working partly while travelling. The Geneva Bible of 1560 was the first complete English Bible with numbered verses throughout.

These divisions are useful but sometimes break a thought in the wrong place. For example, the paragraph that begins at Isa 52:13 belongs with Isa 53, and 1 Cor 13 continues an argument that starts in 1 Cor 12. Reading by paragraphs and whole books helps avoid lifting verses out of context.

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman
sources.title: The Text of the New Testament

sources.author: Christopher de Hamel
sources.title: The Book: A History of the Bible

callout.text: Myth: 'Chapter and verse numbers are part of the inspired text.' Fact: they were added more than a thousand years after the books were written, as a reference system. Different traditions even number some chapters differently (for example Psalm titles, and Mal 4 is chapter 3 in Hebrew Bibles).

views.name: High confidence in the text
views.summary: Held by many evangelical and Catholic textual scholars (for example Daniel Wallace, F. F. Bruce). The abundance and age of the manuscripts let us recover the original wording with very high confidence in almost every verse; the uncertain places are known and do not change any core teaching.

views.name: Cautious or sceptical emphasis
views.summary: Associated with Bart Ehrman and others. The facts are largely agreed, but the early period (before about 200) is thinly documented, scribes did sometimes change texts for theological reasons, and we should be modest about claiming certainty for every word.

views.name: 'Living text' approach
views.summary: Held by scholars such as David Parker and Eldon Epp. Rather than only reconstructing one original, study the variants as evidence of how early communities read and used the texts; the history of the text is itself valuable.

views.name: Majority-text and Textus Receptus defenders
views.summary: A minority view (for example Maurice Robinson for the Byzantine text; some churches for the KJV's Greek base). The majority of later manuscripts, preserved in continuous church use, better represent the original than a few early Egyptian copies.

furtherQuestions: If no original manuscripts survive, what does it mean to say Scripture is inspired?
Why did the early church prefer the codex to the scroll?
Should a translation keep doubtful passages in the main text, in brackets or in footnotes?
How do the Septuagint and the Hebrew text differ, and which did the apostles use?
What difference does reading by paragraphs rather than verses make to Bible study?

title: Why Some Books Were Left Out
question: Who decided which books went into the Bible, when did they decide, and why were books like Enoch, the Gospel of Thomas or the Shepherd of Hermas left out?
plainAnswer: No single person, emperor or council 'picked' the books of the Bible. The list grew out of centuries of use: churches kept reading the books they believed came from the apostles and prophets, were early, taught the faith they had received and were used widely. By the late 300s most churches agreed on the 27 books of the New Testament, and later councils confirmed what was already practice. Christians still disagree about a group of Jewish books (the Apocrypha or deuterocanon), which Catholic and Orthodox churches include and Protestants do not, and the Ethiopian church has a wider canon still. Books such as the Gospel of Thomas or Judas were left out mainly because they were later, not linked to the apostles and taught a different message; the claim that Nicaea or Constantine chose the Bible is a modern myth.
keyTakeaways: The canon formed gradually, by use and recognition, over roughly 300 years; councils mostly confirmed existing practice.
Early Christians asked: is it apostolic, early, faithful to the received faith, widely used and read in church worship?
The Council of Nicaea (325) did not discuss the canon, and Constantine did not choose the books.

The main live disagreement is over the Old Testament Apocrypha/deuterocanon: accepted by Catholics (Trent, 1546) and Orthodox, set apart by Luther and the Anglicans, and rejected as Scripture by the Westminster Confession.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church keeps the largest canon, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees.
Some books that 'nearly made it' (1 Clement, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Didache) were respected and read but finally judged not to be Scripture.
Gnostic gospels such as Thomas and Judas were known to early writers and rejected, not hidden; most scholars date them to the 100s or later.

sections.heading: What 'canon' means and how Christians think about it
sections.body:
'Canon' comes from the Greek kanon, a straight rod used for measuring. Paul uses the word for a 'rule' to walk by (Gal 6:16). By the 300s it meant the fixed list of books read as Scripture.

Traditions explain the canon differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians stress that the church, guided by the Spirit, discerned and defined the canon, so Scripture and church tradition belong together. Protestants generally say the church recognised books that were already authoritative because God inspired them; the church is a witness to the canon, not its source. Historians of every background agree on the basic story: the list emerged gradually through use and was confirmed by later decisions.

The New Testament already shows books being received as authoritative. 1 Thessalonians says the message was received 'as the word of God' (1 Thess 2:13). 1 Timothy quotes a saying found in Luke beside a law of Moses and calls both 'scripture' (1 Tim 5:18), and 2 Peter puts Paul's letters alongside 'the other scriptures' (2 Pet 3:16).

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger
sources.title: The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance

sources.author: F. F. Bruce
sources.title: The Canon of Scripture

callout.text: Did the church create the canon or recognise it? Catholic and Orthodox writers stress the church's authority in defining it; Protestant writers stress that the church only acknowledged what God had given. Both sides accept the same historical facts and differ on their theological meaning. See /debates/scripture-and-tradition.

sections.heading: The tests early Christians used
sections.body:
Early writers did not publish a checklist, but scholars can see several questions at work in what they wrote.

Apostolicity: was the book written by an apostle or a close associate (Mark with Peter, Luke with Paul)? Paul warns about letters falsely claiming to be from him (2 Thess 2:2), so authorship mattered.

Antiquity: did it come from the apostolic age? A book known to be recent was ruled out, even if it was edifying. The Muratorian Fragment says the Shepherd of Hermas was written recently, in the writer's own lifetime, and so should not be read publicly as Scripture.

Orthodoxy: did it agree with the 'rule of faith', the core teaching handed down from the apostles? Paul says even an angel preaching another gospel should be rejected (Gal 1:8-9), and John tells readers to test teachers by whether they confess that Jesus came in the flesh (1 John 4:1-3).

Catholicity: was it accepted widely, not just in one city or sect? Paul's letters were meant to be passed around (Col 4:16).

Church use: had it been read aloud in worship from early on? The books that were read Sunday by Sunday tended to become the canon.

sections.heading: The Old Testament: Jewish and early Christian lists
sections.body:
Jesus speaks of 'the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44) and of the blood of the martyrs 'from Abel to Zacharias' (Luke 11:51), which may reflect a Hebrew order that ends with Chronicles (2 Chr 24:20-22). Around AD 95 the Jewish historian Josephus says the Jews have 22 sacred books, which most scholars match with the 39 books of the Protestant Old Testament counted differently (Against Apion 1.38-41).

Many early Christians read the Greek Septuagint, which included extra books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch and 1-2 Maccabees, plus additions to Esther and Daniel. These are called the 'Apocrypha' ('hidden' books) by Protestants and the 'deuterocanon' ('second canon', meaning recognised later, not less inspired) by Catholics. Some Fathers, such as Melito of Sardis and Athanasius, listed a shorter Old Testament close to the Hebrew one while still valuing the extra books; others, such as Augustine, included them.

callout.text: Myth: 'A Jewish council at Jamnia (Yavneh) closed the Hebrew canon in AD 90.' Fact: this theory, popular in the 1800s and early 1900s, has been largely abandoned. The rabbis at Yavneh discussed whether certain books such as Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs 'defile the hands', but there is no evidence of a council that fixed a list (Jack P. Lewis, Journal of Bible and Religion, 1964).

sections.heading: The New Testament: who decided and when
sections.body:
By about 180 Irenaeus of Lyon defended exactly four Gospels as the church's received books (Against Heresies 3.11.8). The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list usually dated to the late 100s (some scholars argue for the 300s), names most of our New Testament.

Around 325 the church historian Eusebius sorted books into three groups: 'acknowledged' (the Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters, 1 John, 1 Peter), 'disputed' (James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John) and 'spurious' or rejected (Church History 3.25). Revelation he placed uneasily in both camps. Hebrews was accepted in the East but questioned in the West because its author was unknown.

In 367 Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria, in his 39th Festal Letter, listed exactly our 27 books and warned that nothing should be added to them or taken away. In the West, a synod at Rome in 382 is often said to have issued a list (the evidence is disputed), and the North African councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397 and 419), strongly influenced by Augustine, approved the 27 books along with the deuterocanonical books. These were regional councils, not empire-wide ones, but their lists became standard in the West.

Some churches kept differences for centuries. The Syriac Peshitta long lacked 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. Some Greek churches doubted Revelation until the Middle Ages.

sections.heading: The Apocrypha dispute: Jerome, Augustine, Luther, Trent and Westminster
sections.body:
The longest-running disagreement is about the extra Old Testament books.

Jerome, translating the Vulgate around 390-405, learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers and preferred the 'Hebrew truth'. In his preface to Samuel and Kings he said books outside the Hebrew canon should be set among the 'apocrypha', though he still translated some and said the church reads them for edification. Augustine, by contrast, accepted them as canonical because the churches read them (On Christian Doctrine 2.8). The two corresponded and disagreed courteously on translation questions.

At the Reformation Luther's 1534 German Bible gathered these books between the Testaments under a heading saying they are not equal to Holy Scripture but useful and good to read. Luther also moved Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation to the end of his New Testament because he doubted them, though he did not remove them. The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (Article VI, 1563/1571) say the church reads the Apocrypha 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but does not use it to establish doctrine. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 1.3) goes further: these books are no part of Scripture and should be treated like other human writings.

The Catholic Council of Trent, in its fourth session (8 April 1546), formally defined the canon including the deuterocanonical books, under anathema. It was the first time the Western church made the list a matter of solemn dogma, though it repeated the lists of Florence (1442) and the North African councils.

The Orthodox churches accept these books, often calling them 'anagnoskomena' ('those to be read'); the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) affirmed them. Orthodox Bibles also include 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151, with some variation between churches.

callout.text: Myth: 'Catholics added books to the Bible at Trent.' Fact: these books had been in Christian Bibles and lectionaries for over a thousand years; Trent defined them formally. Opposite myth: 'Protestants removed books.' Fact: the Reformers mostly followed Jerome's earlier doubts, and many early Protestant Bibles (including the 1611 KJV) still printed the Apocrypha in a separate section.

sections.heading: The Ethiopian canon and 1 Enoch
sections.body:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has the broadest canon, traditionally counted as 81 books. Besides the deuterocanon it includes 1 Enoch, Jubilees and the three books of Meqabyan (unrelated to the Greek Maccabees), and its New Testament can include church-order books. The exact list is counted in more than one way.

1 Enoch is a Jewish collection of visions about angels, judgement and the end, parts of it dating to the 200s BC. Copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jude quotes it directly (Jude 1:14-15), and some early Christians such as Tertullian defended it (On the Apparel of Women 1.3).

Outside Ethiopia it was set aside because it was not in the Hebrew canon, was widely recognised as written long after Enoch's time, and was later used by groups with unusual teachings about angels. Most Christians read Jude's quotation as citing a respected book for a true point, as Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28), without making the whole book Scripture. The Ethiopian church replies that its long, unbroken use of Enoch is itself a sign of the Spirit's guidance.

sections.heading: Gospels of Thomas, Judas and Peter: why they were rejected
sections.body:
The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings of Jesus with almost no narrative. A complete Coptic copy was found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945; Greek fragments had been found at Oxyrhynchus around 1897-1903. About half its sayings resemble those in the Gospels; others teach that salvation comes through secret knowledge and self-discovery. Most scholars date it in its present form to the 100s; a minority (for example Stephen Patterson) argue that an early layer goes back to the first century. It was rejected because it was not linked with apostolic tradition in the churches' use, was late and taught a different message from the received Gospels.

The Gospel of Judas presents Judas as the only disciple who understood Jesus. Irenaeus mentioned it around 180 as a book of a gnostic group (Against Heresies 1.31.1). A Coptic copy (Codex Tchacos) was published in 2006. It is a 2nd-century gnostic text and was never a candidate for the canon; scholars debate even how positively it portrays Judas.

The Gospel of Peter, an account of the passion with a giant walking cross, was at first allowed by Bishop Serapion of Antioch around 200, who withdrew permission after reading it and finding passages he thought taught that Christ only seemed to suffer (Eusebius, Church History 6.12).

The pattern is the same: these books were known, read and argued about, then judged later and different in teaching from the Gospels already in use.

callout.text: The date of Thomas is a genuine scholarly debate. Most place it in the 100s and see dependence on the canonical Gospels; some argue for independent early sayings. Even scholars who date some sayings early agree that it was not used as Scripture by the mainstream churches.

sections.heading: Books that came close: Hermas, 1 Clement, the Didache, Barnabas
sections.body:
Not every rejected book was heretical. Some were orthodox and loved but finally judged not to be Scripture.

The Shepherd of Hermas, a book of visions about repentance written in Rome, was very popular. Irenaeus quotes it as 'scripture' and it appears in Codex Sinaiticus. But the Muratorian Fragment said it was recent and should be read privately, not in public worship as prophecy or apostle. Tertullian later turned against it over its teaching on forgiveness after baptism.

1 Clement, a letter from the church in Rome to Corinth around 96, was read in some churches and is included in Codex Alexandrinus. The Epistle of Barnabas, with strongly allegorical readings of the Old Testament, appears in Codex Sinaiticus. The Didache, an early church manual, was recommended by Athanasius for new believers alongside Hermas, but explicitly outside the canon.

These books failed mainly on apostolicity and antiquity: they were known to come from after the apostles. Today they are grouped as the 'Apostolic Fathers' and are valued as the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

sections.heading: Myths corrected: Nicaea, Constantine and The Da Vinci Code
sections.body:
A popular story says that the Council of Nicaea (325), under Emperor Constantine, voted on which books to include and burned the rest. The surviving records of Nicaea (its creed, canons and letters) deal with the divinity of Christ (the Arian controversy), the date of Easter and church discipline. They say nothing about the canon.

The story seems to come partly from a late legend, found in a medieval Greek collection (the Synodicon Vetus), that the bishops placed all the books on an altar and the false ones fell to the floor. Voltaire repeated it mockingly in the 1700s, and it spread from there.

Constantine did order 50 fine copies of the Scriptures from Eusebius for the churches of Constantinople around 331 (Life of Constantine 4.36), but nothing suggests he decided their contents; Eusebius's own lists show disputed books were still being debated.

Dan Brown's novel *The Da Vinci Code* (2003) has a character claim that more than 80 gospels were considered and that Constantine commissioned a new Bible that suppressed a human Jesus. Historians across the spectrum, including sceptics such as Bart Ehrman, have pointed out that this is fiction: the four Gospels were already accepted by about 180, and the gnostic gospels, far from portraying a merely human Jesus, usually stress his divinity even more.

views.summary: The church, guided by the Holy Spirit and drawing on apostolic tradition, discerned the canon; Trent's list (73 books) confirms what the church had long read, including the deuterocanon.

views.name: Eastern Orthodox and Oriental churches
views.summary: The canon is part of living tradition received in worship. The wider Old Testament is read in church; boundaries are less sharply defined, and the Ethiopian church keeps 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

views.name: Protestant
views.summary: God's inspired books carry their own authority and the church recognised them. The Old Testament canon is the Hebrew one Jesus and the apostles received; the Apocrypha may be read with profit (Lutheran, Anglican) or treated as ordinary human writing (Reformed, Westminster).

views.name: Critical-historical
views.summary: Historians describe the canon as the outcome of social, theological and practical factors over centuries, with real diversity in early Christianity; many hold that the canonical books are nonetheless the earliest and most widely used sources.

title: Types, Shadows and Symbols
question: The New Testament says the Passover lamb, the bronze serpent and Jonah point to Jesus. How do we read types and symbols wisely without making the Bible say whatever we like?
plainAnswer: A 'type' is a real person, event or institution in the Old Testament that God's later action in Christ echoes and fulfils, the way a shadow hints at the shape of the thing that casts it. The New Testament itself reads the Bible this way, calling the Passover, the bronze serpent and Jonah pictures of Jesus. Allegory is different: it treats the details of a text as a code for spiritual ideas, often with little regard for history. Christians have argued for centuries about how far to go, from the bold spiritual readings of Alexandria to the more historical approach of Antioch and the medieval 'four senses'. Most teachers today use some simple guardrails: start with the plain meaning, look for New Testament warrant, check for real correspondence and a 'greater fulfilment', and never build a doctrine on a symbol alone.
keyTakeaways: Typology links real historical events and persons by God's pattern of action; allegory reads details as coded meanings.
The New Testament uses the words 'type' (tupos) and 'shadow' for Old Testament realities that point forward (Rom 5:14; Heb 10:1).
Alexandria (Origen) favoured spiritual and allegorical readings; Antioch (Chrysostom, Theodore) stressed history and the plain sense, though the contrast is often overdrawn.
The medieval 'four senses' (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical) were meant to grow from the literal sense, not replace it.
Good guardrails: plain sense first, New Testament warrant, real correspondence, escalation to something greater, and no doctrine resting on a symbol alone.
Numbers in Revelation (7, 12, 144,000, 666, 1,000) are widely agreed to be symbolic in some way, but how far that goes is debated.

sections.heading: What typology is
sections.body:
The New Testament writers believed God acts in patterns. What he did with Adam, the exodus, the temple or the kings was real history, and it also foreshadowed what he would do in Christ. The Greek word tupos means an impression or pattern, like the mark a seal leaves in wax. Paul calls Adam 'the figure (tupos) of him that was to come' (Rom 5:14) and says the events of the exodus happened as 'examples' (tupoi) for us (1 Cor 10:6, 1 Cor 10:11).

Hebrews uses the language of shadow and reality: the tabernacle was a copy and shadow of heavenly things (Heb 8:5), and the law had 'a shadow of good things to come' (Heb 10:1). Paul says festivals and sabbaths were 'a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ' (Col 2:16-17). Peter calls baptism the antitype of the flood (1 Pet 3:20-21).

So typology has three parts: the type (the earlier reality), the antitype (the fulfilment) and the link between them, which is God's consistent way of acting. Jesus himself reads Scripture this way when he says the scriptures testify of him (John 5:39) and explains from 'all the scriptures' the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27).

sources.title: Typos: The Typological Interpretation of the Old Testament in the New

sources.title: Typology in Scripture: A Study of Hermeneutical Tupos Structures

sections.heading: Typology versus allegory
sections.body:
Allegory reads a text as a coded story where each detail stands for an idea. The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria, a contemporary of Jesus, read the patriarchs as stages of the soul's journey. Many Christian writers adopted similar methods: for example, an early reading of the Good Samaritan made the inn the church and the two coins the two sacraments or the two Testaments.

Typology differs in two ways. First, it takes the history seriously: the exodus really happened, and that is why it can foreshadow redemption. Second, it links whole patterns (a deliverance, a sacrifice, a king), not every small detail.

The line is not perfectly sharp. Paul calls his reading of Sarah and Hagar an allegory (Gal 4:24), yet it works much like typology, contrasting two covenants. Paul also reads the law about not muzzling an ox as being 'for our sakes' (1 Cor 9:9-10). Scholars debate whether these are typology, allegory or something in between.

sources.title: Biblical Exegesis and the Formation of Christian Culture

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.title: Questions on the Gospels

callout.text: Myth: 'The church fathers just made things up with allegory.' Fact: most fathers held that spiritual readings had to agree with the rule of faith and with clear Scripture elsewhere. Their readings can seem fanciful to us, but they worked within limits, and many of their typological insights come straight from the New Testament.

sections.heading: Alexandria and Antioch: two schools of reading
sections.body:
In the early church two centres became associated with different styles. In Alexandria, Origen (c. 185-254) taught that Scripture, like a human being, has a body, a soul and a spirit: a literal sense, a moral sense and a spiritual sense (On First Principles 4.2.4). Where the literal sense seemed unworthy of God or impossible, he looked for a spiritual meaning.

In Antioch, teachers such as Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia and John Chrysostom pressed for close attention to history, grammar and the author's purpose. They accepted typology but spoke of theoria, a spiritual insight that grows out of the historical meaning rather than leaping past it. Theodore was cautious about reading many psalms as directly about Christ.

Many scholars, notably Frances Young, now argue that the contrast is overdrawn: both schools used typology and spiritual reading, and their differences were partly about rhetorical style and theological debates. The two names remain a useful shorthand for two instincts every reader has: 'see Christ everywhere' and 'first hear what the text meant then'.

sections.heading: The four senses (the quadriga)
sections.body:
In the medieval West, reading settled into four 'senses' of Scripture, sometimes called the quadriga (a four-horse chariot). John Cassian (c. 420) gave the classic example of Jerusalem (Conferences 14.8): literally a city in Judea; allegorically the church; morally (tropologically) the human soul; and anagogically (pointing upward) the heavenly city of God.

A short medieval rhyme, usually credited to Augustine of Dacia (c. 1260), summed it up: the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral sense what to do, and anagogy where we are heading.

Thomas Aquinas insisted that all the spiritual senses are founded on the literal one, and that arguments for doctrine must come from the literal sense alone (Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10). The Catholic Catechism still teaches the four senses with that priority (paragraphs 115-119).

The Reformers pushed hard for the 'literal sense', meaning the sense the author intended, including figures of speech. Yet Luther and Calvin kept a strong typology, especially seeing Christ in the Psalms and the sacrificial system. Eastern Orthodox reading never formalised the four senses but continues the patristic habit of reading the Old Testament in the light of Christ, especially in its hymns.

sections.heading: Guardrails for reading types and symbols
sections.body:
Most interpreters, across traditions, use some version of these checks.

1. Plain sense first. Ask what the passage meant to its first readers before asking what it foreshadows.

2. New Testament warrant. Is the link made explicitly in the New Testament (Passover, bronze serpent, Jonah, Melchizedek), implied (Joseph rejected by his brothers then exalted), traditional (Isaac carrying the wood), or only someone's idea? The more speculative, the lighter the weight. The Anglican bishop Herbert Marsh (1820s) argued we should only call something a type if the New Testament does; most now think that is too narrow, since the apostles were showing a method, not giving a complete list.

3. Real correspondence. The type and antitype should share a significant pattern, not just a word or a colour.

4. Escalation. The fulfilment is greater than the shadow: 'a greater than Jonas is here', 'a greater than Solomon' (Matt 12:41-42). If the 'antitype' is no greater, it is probably just a parallel.

5. No doctrine from symbols alone. A teaching should rest on clear statements; types illustrate and deepen it.

6. Watch for differences. Every type also differs from Christ, and noticing the differences keeps us honest (Hebrews does this constantly: Heb 7:23-28).

sources.title: Handbook on the New Testament Use of the Old Testament

callout.text: How Christ-centred should Old Testament reading be? Some (redemptive-historical and many patristic readers) see Christ foreshadowed across the whole Old Testament; others warn that this can mute the text's own voice and its meaning for Israel. See /debates/christocentric-hermeneutic.

sections.heading: Worked example: the Passover lamb
sections.body:
The type: in Egypt each Israelite household killed a spotless lamb, put its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passed over those houses (Exod 12:1-13). No bone of the lamb was to be broken (Exod 12:46). The meal was repeated every year as a memorial.

The antitype: John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' (John 1:29). John's Gospel places Jesus' death at the time the Passover lambs were sacrificed and notes that none of his bones were broken, citing the Passover rule (John 19:36). Paul says plainly, 'Christ our passover is sacrificed for us' (1 Cor 5:7). Jesus himself reshaped the Passover meal into the Lord's Supper (Luke 22:14-20).

Warrant: explicit. Correspondence: a substitute death, protection by blood, deliverance from slavery, a memorial meal. Escalation: from one night's rescue in Egypt to deliverance from sin and death for the world.

Differences: the Passover lamb was not, in Exodus, mainly a sin offering; it was a sign of protection and belonging. Readers who notice this see that the New Testament gathers several Old Testament sacrifices into one picture of Christ.

sources.author: Melito of Sardis
sources.title: On Pascha

sections.heading: Worked example: the bronze serpent, and when a symbol becomes an idol
sections.body:
The type: in the wilderness, Israel complained, and poisonous snakes bit the people. God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole; whoever looked at it lived (Num 21:4-9).

The antitype: Jesus tells Nicodemus that as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that whoever believes may have eternal life (John 3:14-15). The correspondence is striking: the cure looks like the curse, it is lifted up, and the response is simply to look in trust. Early Christians such as Justin Martyr developed the link further (Dialogue with Trypho 91, 94).

A warning comes in the Old Testament itself. Centuries later Israel was burning incense to the bronze serpent, which had been named Nehushtan, and King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kgs 18:4). The object that once pointed to God's mercy had become an object of worship. Types and symbols are signposts; treating the sign as the destination is the danger.

sources.author: Justin Martyr
sources.title: Dialogue with Trypho

sections.heading: Worked example: the sign of Jonah
sections.body:
The type: Jonah was swallowed by a great fish and was in its belly three days and three nights before being spat out on dry land (Jonah 1:17, Jonah 2:10). He then preached to Nineveh, which repented (Jonah 3:5).

The antitype: asked for a sign, Jesus says no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights 'in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:39-40). He adds that Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and 'a greater than Jonas is here' (Matt 12:41). Luke's version focuses on Jonah as a sign to Nineveh through his preaching (Luke 11:29-32).

Escalation is explicit. The 'three days and three nights' phrase raises a question, since Jesus was in the tomb from Friday to Sunday. Many scholars note that Jewish reckoning counted any part of a day as a day, so this is a set phrase rather than 72 hours; a minority argue for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion.

Whether Jonah's story is literal history or a God-inspired parable is debated among Christians; Jesus' use of it as a type works either way for some readers, while others argue that his comparison with the real men of Nineveh implies history.

callout.text: Three days and three nights: most interpreters read it as an idiom for parts of three days (compare Esth 4:16 with Esth 5:1). A minority propose a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion to fit 72 hours.

sections.heading: Worked example: numbers in Revelation
sections.body:
Revelation is full of numbers, and nearly all interpreters agree that at least some are symbolic. Revelation itself explains symbols at times: the seven stars are the angels of seven churches and the lampstands are the churches (Rev 1:20).

Seven suggests completeness (seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls), echoing the seven days of creation. Twelve recalls the tribes and the apostles; the New Jerusalem has twelve gates and twelve foundations (Rev 21:12-14) and measures 12,000 stadia (Rev 21:16). The 144,000 (Rev 7:4, Rev 14:1) is 12 x 12 x 1,000; many read it as the whole people of God, others as a literal number of Jewish believers or a special group. Right after hearing the number, John sees 'a great multitude, which no man could number' (Rev 7:9), which many take as the same group seen differently.

666 is called 'the number of a man' (Rev 13:18). In ancient practice letters had number values (gematria). Many scholars note that 'Nero Caesar' written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666, and a variant reading 616, known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.1) and found in an early papyrus, matches the Latin spelling. Others read 666 as falling short of seven again and again. The 1,000 years (Rev 20:2-7) is read literally by premillennialists and symbolically by amillennialists and many postmillennialists.

The caution: Revelation's numbers invite us to see patterns of completeness, God's people and evil's imitation, not to calculate dates or decode news headlines.

title: Living with Scriptural Paradox
question: The Bible says God is sovereign and that we are responsible, that we are saved by faith and that faith without works is dead, that Jesus is equal with the Father and that the Father is greater. Are these contradictions, and how should we live with them?
plainAnswer: The Bible often puts two truths side by side that seem to pull against each other. A paradox is an apparent clash between two statements that are both true in their proper sense; a contradiction is when two statements cannot both be true in the same sense at the same time. Christians have handled these tensions in several ways: by careful distinctions that show the clash is only apparent (harmonisation), by accepting both truths without fully reconciling them (what J. I. Packer called an antinomy), by confessing that God is beyond our concepts (Eastern 'apophatic' theology), or by reading the different voices as a deliberate conversation within Scripture. Sceptics argue that some tensions are real contradictions between different human authors. Living well with paradox usually means holding both truths in practice, rather than letting one quietly cancel the other.
keyTakeaways: A paradox is an apparent contradiction; a real contradiction affirms and denies the same thing in the same sense at the same time.
Many biblical tensions (sovereignty and responsibility, faith and works, divine and human in Christ) are central to Christian faith, not marginal puzzles.
J. I. Packer's 'antinomy' means two well-attested truths we cannot yet reconcile but must both believe and act on.
G. K. Chesterton argued that Christianity's health lies in keeping opposite truths both at full strength rather than blending them into a weak compromise.
Eastern Orthodox apophatic theology says God exceeds our concepts, so some tensions are signs of mystery, not error.
Harmonisation and literary readings help, but each has a risk: forced explanations on one side, or giving up the unity of Scripture on the other.
In practice, most paradoxes are 'lived' by praying as if all depends on God and acting as if all depends on us, or similar double commitments.

sections.heading: Why the Bible holds truths in tension
sections.body:
Scripture often says two things that seem hard to fit together. Joseph's brothers meant evil, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). Jesus was handed over by God's set purpose, yet the people who crucified him were guilty (Acts 2:23). Paul tells believers to work out their salvation because God works in them (Phil 2:12-13). Jesus says whoever wants to save his life will lose it (Matt 16:25), and Paul says, 'when I am weak, then am I strong' (2 Cor 12:10).

Some tensions sit next to each other on purpose. Proverbs says 'Answer not a fool according to his folly' and in the next verse 'Answer a fool according to his folly' (Prov 26:4-5). The editors plainly saw the clash; the point is that wisdom means knowing which applies when.

There are several reasons for this. God is greater than human understanding (Isa 55:8-9). Reality itself is complex, and truths about persons, love and freedom rarely fit into one formula. And Scripture was written over many centuries in many genres, so it speaks from more than one angle.

sections.heading: Paradox or contradiction?
sections.body:
In logic, a contradiction affirms and denies the same thing in the same sense at the same time: 'this door is open' and 'this door is not open'. Both cannot be true. A paradox is a statement or pair of statements that seem contradictory but, on reflection, may both be true because they speak in different senses or about different aspects.

'I am the vine' and 'I am the door' do not contradict, because they are images. 'My Father is greater than I' (John 14:28) and 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30) were explained by the early church as speaking of Christ's human nature or his role as Son on the one hand, and his divine nature or shared being on the other.

The key questions are: are the two statements using words in the same sense? Are they about the same subject in the same respect? Are they answering the same question? Many apparent contradictions dissolve under these questions; some remain mysterious; and critics argue that some are real.

sources.author: Aristotle
sources.title: Metaphysics

callout.text: Two opposite myths. 'Paradox is just a polite word for contradiction' ignores that many paradoxes rest on real distinctions. 'Calling it a mystery ends the discussion' ignores that Christian thinkers have always worked hard to understand mysteries as far as they can.

sections.heading: Antinomy: J. I. Packer on sovereignty and evangelism
sections.body:
In *Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God* (1961), the Anglican theologian J. I. Packer asked how a Calvinist, who believes God chooses who will be saved, can evangelise urgently. His answer, in chapter 2, used the word 'antinomy'. He defined it (in paraphrase) as an apparent incompatibility between two truths that are each clearly taught and well grounded, which we cannot reconcile with our present understanding but must both accept.

Packer compared it to light behaving both as waves and as particles: physicists accept both because the evidence requires it. In the same way, Scripture teaches both divine sovereignty (Rom 9:15-16, Eph 1:11) and human responsibility to repent and believe (Acts 17:30, Rom 10:13-14). He urged Christians to pray as those who depend entirely on God and to preach as those who must persuade people.

Critics come from two directions. Some Reformed thinkers (for example Gordon Clark) objected that 'antinomy' sounds like an admission of irrationality and preferred to say the tension is resolved in God's mind and partly in ours. Arminian and Wesleyan theologians argue that the tension is largely of Calvinism's own making and is better resolved by understanding election through foreknowledge and grace that enables free response. Many compatibilists, such as D. A. Carson, defend the coherence of the two truths more fully than Packer did.

sections.heading: Chesterton: keeping both truths at full strength
sections.body:
In *Orthodoxy* (1908), G. K. Chesterton described his discovery that Christianity was attacked from opposite sides: too gloomy and too optimistic, too meek and too warlike. In chapter 6, 'The Paradoxes of Christianity', he concluded that the faith did not settle for a bland middle point between such opposites. Instead it held both extremes at full strength side by side: intense humility about ourselves and intense dignity as God's image-bearers; fierce hatred of sin and great love for the sinner.

For Chesterton, the doctrine of Christ is the model: not half God and half man, but fully both (John 1:14, Col 2:9). Heresy, in his picture, usually takes one true idea and lets it run without its balancing partner.

Chesterton was writing as a literary apologist, not a technical theologian, and some readers think he made paradox sound easier and more romantic than it is. But his idea that health lies in balance, not dilution, has shaped much popular Christian thinking.

sections.heading: The Eastern way: apophatic theology and mystery
sections.body:
Eastern Orthodox theology has long stressed 'apophatic' or negative theology: saying what God is not, because God is beyond every human concept. God 'dwells in the light which no man can approach unto' (1 Tim 6:16). Moses drew near 'unto the thick darkness where God was' (Exod 20:21).

Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Life of Moses* (around 390), read Moses' climb into the dark cloud as the soul's growth into God, where knowing God means realising he surpasses knowledge. The writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius (around 500) in *The Mystical Theology* taught that we rise to God by stripping away even our best words. In the 20th century Vladimir Lossky, in *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church*, argued that the doctrines of the Trinity and of Christ are 'antinomies' that guard mystery rather than explain it away.

On this view, tensions such as one God in three persons are not puzzles waiting for a clever solution but boundaries that keep us from shrinking God. Western theology has its own apophatic tradition (Augustine, Aquinas, the medieval mystics), but it has usually been more willing to press for rational explanation. Critics warn that apophatic language can become an excuse for vagueness; its defenders reply that it always goes together with positive (cataphatic) confession of what God has revealed.

sections.heading: Harmonisation: careful distinctions
sections.body:
Harmonisation means showing that two statements fit together once we read them carefully. Augustine wrote *The Harmony of the Gospels* (around 400) to show that differences between the four Gospels were not contradictions.

A classic case is faith and works. Paul says a person is justified by faith 'without the deeds of the law' (Rom 3:28), using Abraham as his example (Rom 4:2-3). James says 'by works a man is justified, and not by faith only' (Jas 2:24), also citing Abraham (Jas 2:21). Most interpreters, Catholic and Protestant, argue that the two use 'works' and 'justify' differently: Paul rejects works of the law as a way to earn standing with God, while James rejects a 'faith' that is only words and shows that real faith proves itself in action. Paul himself says believers are created 'unto good works' (Eph 2:8-10). Catholic and Protestant theologians still differ over how works relate to final justification.

Harmonisation is a natural reading strategy; we do it with any trusted witness. Its risk is forcing. A famous example: the Reformation-era scholar Andreas Osiander is reported to have proposed that Peter denied Jesus six times to fit every Gospel detail. Most harmonisers today prefer to admit where we do not know, rather than invent solutions the texts do not suggest.

callout.text: Myth: 'Paul and James flatly contradict each other, and Luther threw James out.' Fact: most interpreters across traditions see the two addressing different errors with different senses of the words. Luther did call James 'an epistle of straw' compared with Paul's letters in his 1522 preface and doubted its authority, but he kept it in his Bible.

sections.heading: Literary and critical readings: a conversation in the canon
sections.body:
Many scholars read some tensions as deliberate dialogue. Proverbs teaches that wise living generally brings blessing; Job and Ecclesiastes push back that life does not always work that way (Job 21:7, Eccl 9:11). Brevard Childs's 'canonical' approach reads such books as placed together on purpose, so that each corrects and completes the others. Walter Brueggemann describes Israel's 'core testimony' about God's faithfulness alongside a 'countertestimony' of lament and protest, both kept in Scripture.

Historical-critical scholars also explain some tensions by different sources or later rethinking. 2 Samuel says the Lord moved David to number Israel (2 Sam 24:1); the later Chronicles says Satan provoked him (1 Chr 21:1). Many scholars see a development in how Israel spoke about evil and God's role. Traditional readers often see layered causation: God permitted, Satan incited, David chose, as in Job 1-2.

Sceptics such as Bart Ehrman (*Jesus, Interrupted*, 2009) argue that some differences are genuine contradictions between human authors and should be accepted as such. Many believing scholars accept the presence of diverse voices but argue that diversity is not the same as contradiction, and that the canon holds them together intentionally.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.body:
One God, three persons. 'The Lord our God is one Lord' (Deut 6:4), yet Father, Son and Spirit are named together (Matt 28:19). The church did not resolve this by dividing God into three gods or by making the persons masks of one, but by confessing one being (ousia) in three persons (hypostases). The words mark the boundary of the mystery more than they explain it.

Fully God and fully man. Jesus grows tired and hungry (John 4:6) and is worshipped as Lord and God (John 20:28). The Council of Chalcedon (451) said he is one person in two natures, 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.

Already and not yet. Believers have been raised with Christ (Col 3:1) and yet groan waiting for redemption (Rom 8:23). The kingdom has come (Luke 11:20) and we pray 'thy kingdom come' (Matt 6:10). Most scholars describe this as the overlap of the ages, not a contradiction.

Strength in weakness. Christ's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9-10). This is a paradox of experience: God's way often runs through loss, as the cross itself shows (1 Cor 1:25).

sections.heading: Living with paradox day to day
sections.body:
Paradoxes are not only for theologians. They shape prayer and action. A common Christian saying (with many versions and attributions) is to pray as if everything depends on God and work as if everything depends on you. Nehemiah did both: 'we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night' (Neh 4:9).

Two errors are easy. One is rationalism: dropping one truth because it does not fit our system (for example denying responsibility because God is sovereign). The other is lazy mystery: calling everything a paradox so we never think hard. Jesus' own advice to be 'wise as serpents, and harmless as doves' (Matt 10:16) is itself a call to hold two qualities together.

Practical steps: state both truths in the Bible's own words; ask whether different senses or subjects are involved; read how different traditions handle it; and notice which truth you tend to neglect, then lean into it. Humility helps: Paul ends his hardest argument about election not with a formula but with worship (Rom 11:33-36).

callout.text: The 'pray as if... work as if...' saying is often attributed to Augustine or to Ignatius of Loyola. Neither attribution is secure in that exact form, so it is best quoted as a traditional saying.

views.name: Reformed (antinomy and compatibilism)
views.summary: God's sovereignty and human responsibility are both fully true; some (Packer) call this an antinomy we cannot resolve, others (Carson) argue they are compatible though not fully explained.

views.name: Arminian and Wesleyan
views.summary: Many alleged paradoxes about salvation dissolve once God's grace is seen as enabling a real free response; mystery remains, but a sovereign God freely chooses to give people genuine freedom.

views.name: Catholic and Thomist
views.summary: Faith and reason cannot contradict; careful distinctions (primary and secondary causes, nature and grace) show how truths fit, while the highest mysteries exceed reason without opposing it.

views.name: Eastern Orthodox
views.summary: Antinomies in doctrine protect the mystery of God; they are to be contemplated and worshipped, not solved, with apophatic humility alongside confession of revealed truth.

views.name: Critical-sceptical
views.summary: Some biblical tensions are genuine contradictions between different authors and periods; acknowledging them is part of reading the Bible historically.
